'''unbonnet''' (un-bon′et), ''v.'' '''I.''' ''intrans.'' To uncover the head by taking off the bonnet or, by extension, any head-dress. ''Scott'', L. of the L., v. 17.

'''II.''' ''trans.'' To remove the bonnet or, by extension, any head-dress from, as the head, or the wearer of the head-dress.

'''unbonneted''' (un-bon′et-ed), ''a.'' '''1.''' Having no bonnet on; by extension, without any head-dress; bareheaded.

{{smaller block|''Unbonneted'' he runs. {{right|''Shak.'', Lear, iii. 1. 14.}}}}

'''2.''' Without taking the bonnet or cap off; making no obeisance.

From men of royal siege, and my demerits

As this that I have reach’d.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Othello, i. 2. 23.}}}}

'''unbowed''' (un-boud′), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unbowed''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''bowed'', pp. of ''bow''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.''] '''1.''' Not bowed or arched; not bent.

'''unbowel†''' (un-bou′el), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''bowel.''] To deprive of the entrails; eviscerate; disembowel. ''Dr. H. More.''

'''unbrace''' (un-brās′), ''v.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''brace.''] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To remove the points or braces of; free from tension or constraint; loose; relax: as, to ''unbrace'' a drum; to ''unbrace'' the arms; to ''unbrace'' the nerves.

'''unbookish''' (un-bu̇k′ish), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not addicted to books or reading.
{{smaller block|It is to be wondered how museless ''unbookish'' they were, minding nought but the feats of war. {{right|''Milton.''}}}}
'''2.''' Not cultivated by study; unlearned.
{{smaller block|<poem>His ''unbookish'' jealousy must construe
Poor Cassio’s smiles, gestures, and light behaviour
Quite in the wrong.</poem>{{right|''Shak.'', Othello, iv. 1. 102.}}}}

'''unbooklearned''' (un-bu̇k′lėr″ned), ''a.'' Illiterate. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|''Un-book-learn’d'' people have conn’d by heart many psalms of the old translation. {{right|''Fuller'', Ch. Hist., VII. i. 32. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''unbore†''', ''a.'' A Middle English form of ''unborn.'' ''Gower'', Conf. Amant., vi.

'''unborn''' (un-bôrn′), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unboren'', ''unbore''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''born''<sup>1</sup>.] Not born; not brought into life; not yet existing.
{{smaller block|<poem>The woe’s to come; the children yet ''unborn''
Shall feel this day as sharp to them as thorn.</poem>{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. II., iv. 1. 322.}}}}

'''unbosom''' (un-bu̇z′um), ''v.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''bosom.''] '''I.''' ''trans.'' To reveal in confidence; disclose, as one’s secret opinions or feelings: often used with a reflexive pronoun.
{{smaller block|<poem>Their several counsels they ''unbosom'' shall.</poem>{{right|''Shak.'', L. L. L., v. 2. 141.}}}}
{{smaller block|The rest of this winter I spent in a lonesome, solitary life, having none to converse with, none to ''unbosom myself'' unto, none to ask counsel of, none to seek relief from, but the Lord alone, who yet was more than all. {{right|''T. Ellwood'', Life (ed. Howells), p. 227.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To make a revelation in confidence; disclose one’s innermost feelings.
{{smaller block|Princes usually treat such persons familiarly; and, quitting their throne like Luna, think they may with safety ''unbosom'' to them.{{right|''Bacon'', Political Fables, iv., Expl.}}}}

'''unbosomer''' (un-bu̇z′um-ėr), ''n.'' One who unbosoms, discloses, or reveals.
{{smaller block|An ''unbosomer'' of secrets.{{right|''Thackeray.''}}}}

'''unbottomed''' (un-bot′umd), ''a.'' '''1.''' Having no bottom; bottomless.
{{smaller block|<poem>The dark, ''unbottom’d'', infinite abyss.</poem>{{right|''Milton'', P. L., ii. 405.}}}}
'''2†.''' Having no solid foundation; having no reliance.
{{smaller block|This is a special act of Christian hope, to be thus ''unbottomed'' of ourselves, and fastened upon God.{{right|''Hammond.''}}}}

'''unbought''' (un-bât′), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unbouht'', ''unbocht'', ''unboht'', < AS. ''unboht''; as ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''bought''<sup>2</sup>.] '''1.''' Not bought; obtained without money or purchase.
{{smaller block|<poem>The ''unbought'' dainties of the poor.</poem>{{right|''Dryden'', Horace, Epod. 2.}} The wide, the ''unbounded'' prospect.
{{right|''Addison'', Cato, v. 1.}}}}
'''2.''' Having no check or control; unrestrained.
{{smaller block|<poem>He was a man
Of an ''unbounded'' stomach, ever ranking
Himself with princes. ''Shak.'', Hen. VIII., iv. 2. 34.</poem>}}
='''Syn. 1.''' {{smaller|Boundless, illimitable.—'''2.''' Uncontrolled.}}

'''unboundedly''' (un-boun′ded-li), ''adv.'' In an unbounded manner; without bounds or limits. ''Byron.''

'''unboundedness''' (un-boun′ded-nes), ''n.'' The state or condition of being unbounded; freedom from bounds or limits; specifically, that character of a continuum by virtue of which, if any point be taken, and then any other indefinitely near the first, a third point may be found indefinitely near the first, and situated opposite to the second with reference to the first.
{{smaller block|In the extension of space-construction to the infinitely great we must distinguish between ''unboundedness'' and infinite extent; the former belonging to the extent relations, the latter to the measure relations. That space is an unbounded three-fold manifoldness is an assumption which is developed by every conception of the outer world; according to which at every instant the region of real perception is completed and the possible positions of a sought object are constructed, and which by these applications is forever confirming itself. The ''unboundedness'' of space possesses in this way a greater empirical certainty than any external experience. But its infinite extent by no means follows from this.
{{right|''Riemann'', tr. by Clifford.}}}}

'''unbounden†''' (un-boun′dẹn), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unbounden''; pp. of ''unbind'', ''v.''] Set free; unwedded.
{{smaller block|<poem>Were I ''unbounden'', also mote I thee,
I wolde never eft comen in the snare.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Prol. to Merchant’s Tale, l. 14.}}}}

{{smaller block|God keep all vows ''unbroke'' that swear to thee!
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. II., iv. 1. 215.}}
By age ''unbroke.'' {{right|''Pope'', Odyssey, viii. 147.}}}}

{{smaller block|The clergy met very punctually, and the patriarch’s letter was produced in the assembly, the seal examined, and declared to be the patriarch’s and ''unbroken.''
{{right|''Bruce'', Source of the Nile, II. 460.}}}}
